The energy of the detected line is  

\[
E_{\text{obs}} = 3.9\times10^{-6}\ \text{eV}.
\]

The well‑known hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen (the 21 cm line) has a rest‑frame energy  

\[
E_{0}=h\nu_{0}=h(1.420\,\text{GHz})\approx5.9\times10^{-6}\ \text{eV}.
\]

If this line is observed from a source at a cosmological distance, its energy is reduced by the redshift factor:

\[
E_{\text{obs}} = \frac{E_{0}}{1+z}\;\Longrightarrow\;1+z = \frac{E_{0}}{E_{\text{obs}}}
               \approx \frac{5.9}{3.9}\approx1.5,
\]
so \(z\approx0.5\). A redshift of about 0.5 corresponds to a comoving distance of roughly 2 Gpc, matching the given distance. Hence the line being detected is almost certainly the 21 cm hyperfine line of neutral hydrogen (HI).

In the Milky Way the 21 cm line is seen in **absorption** only when the HI is cold and dense enough to produce a significant optical depth; the warm neutral medium is too low‑density to give strong absorption and is seen mainly in emission. Therefore the absorption counterpart of this line would arise from the **cold atomic interstellar medium** (the cold neutral medium).

Thus the most appropriate choice is:

**Answer: C**.
